name: Pale Vinaceous-Fawn
lede: Pale Vinaceous-Fawn is a dusty, pinkish tan, the pale tone Robert Ridgway charted beside the parent color Vinaceous-Fawn in his 1912 color atlas, and a near-exact match for the everyday name Oatmeal.

sections.title: A pale tone of Vinaceous-Fawn
sections.body:
Pale Vinaceous-Fawn puts Ridgway's tone word Pale in front of [[vinaceous-fawn]], a compound built from *vinaceous*, Ridgway's own word for a wine-tinted hue, and fawn, a pale brown [1]. Vinaceous-Fawn itself is Ridgway's plate XL, hue 13 triple-prime, tone b; it never reached the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 or Maerz and Paul's 1930 list, staying a Ridgway-only name [1].

On screen this swatch sits close enough to [[oatmeal]] to read as the same color, a zero-unit match [1]; its nearest distinct neighbor is [[sandust]], 3.6 units off [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 1,420 of 23,781 paintings, 5.97 percent, as photographed; narrowing to at least five percent coverage inside a painting leaves 1,031, more common than 90 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It peaks in the 1100s, present in 12.0 percent of the 50 paintings we have from then, 1.8 times the archive's overall rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light across its 1,031 appearances by lightness rank [2].

The earliest match dates to 900, in a work attributed to Zhao Guangfu, a floor and not a first since the archive's early centuries are thin; that is 1,012 years before the name's 1912 record, so the match marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2]. Xugu used it most, in 9 of his 16 paintings here, 6.4 times the rate of the museums those works come from, and it is most over-represented in paintings from China, 2.1 times the expected rate [2].
